title: Computational Cortical Columns
intro: A learning path from the biology of the neocortical column to building one out of spiking neurons — with simulations you can play with along the way.

blocks.text: The neocortex is a sheet of tissue, roughly 2 to 4 mm thick in humans, folded into the outer layer of the mammalian brain. Under the microscope, regions that handle vision, touch, language or planning look surprisingly alike: the same six layers, the same cell types, the same wiring motifs repeated side by side. In 1957 Vernon Mountcastle found that neurons in a vertical column through somatosensory cortex share response properties, and in 1978 he proposed that the column is the basic repeating unit of the cortex and that every region runs essentially the same algorithm. If that is true, understanding one column — well enough to build it — would go a long way towards understanding intelligence.

A computational cortical column is a model of that repeating unit: a population of model neurons, organised the way cortical tissue is organised, that learns from a stream of sensory input without labels. Different research programmes disagree about what the column computes. Numenta's Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) says it learns sequences and predicts its next input; the Thousand Brains Theory adds that each column learns whole objects by pairing features with locations, and that columns vote; predictive-coding models say it sends prediction errors up a hierarchy; large-scale simulations such as the Potjans–Diesmann microcircuit and the Blue Brain reconstruction try to reproduce the circuit first and ask questions later. This topic covers all of them, so you can borrow the parts you need.

The sections are ordered as a learning path: each one uses ideas from the ones before it. Read them in order the first time; later, jump straight to the page you need. Each page starts with intuition, then gives the math, then says what it means when you build a column, and ends with its sources. Highlight any term to see its definition — the glossary covers the vocabulary of this topic.

items: 1. Biology of the Neocortex — layers L1–L6, minicolumns, cell types, thalamocortical loops, and Mountcastle's hypothesis. What you are trying to copy, and which details matter.
2. Spiking Neuron Models — leaky integrate-and-fire, Izhikevich, Hodgkin–Huxley, synapses, and active dendrites with NMDA spikes. Interactive: a LIF neuron with adjustable input and parameters.

3. Plasticity and Learning — Hebbian learning, STDP, homeostasis, inhibition and k-winners-take-all, and sparse distributed representations. Interactive: an STDP explorer, a spiking layer with k-WTA, and an SDR overlap calculator.
4. Hierarchical Temporal Memory — the HTM neuron, the spatial pooler, temporal memory, and sequence prediction with distal dendrites. Interactive: a temporal-memory sequence-learning demo.

5. The Thousand Brains Theory — reference frames, grid and displacement cells, sensorimotor object recognition, voting between columns, and Monty. Interactive: multi-column voting for object recognition.
6. Other Column Models — the canonical microcircuit, predictive coding, the Potjans–Diesmann microcircuit, and Blue Brain.

7. Building an SNN Column — simulators (Brian2, NEST, Nengo, Norse, snnTorch, Lava), neuromorphic hardware (Loihi, SpiNNaker and others), encoding schemes, evaluation, a step-by-step roadmap, and common pitfalls.
8. Key Papers and Reading List — annotated citations by theme, with where to start.

blocks.text: Three ideas to keep in mind

items: Sparse and distributed. At any moment only a few percent of cortical neurons are strongly active, and meaning is carried by which ones. Sparse distributed representations make codes robust to noise and let a neuron recognise a pattern from a small sample of it.

Prediction through dendrites. Pyramidal neurons have thousands of synapses, most of them far from the cell body on dendrites that can generate their own local spikes. HTM and the Thousand Brains Theory propose that these distal inputs put a cell into a predictive state, so that the cell fires a little earlier — and wins the competition — when its prediction comes true.

Many columns, one percept. In the Thousand Brains view each column builds its own model of the objects it senses, using a location signal like that of grid cells, and columns reach a consensus through long-range lateral connections. Intelligence is then the product of thousands of similar models working in parallel rather than one central model.

blocks.text: Much of this field is still open. The anatomy in Section 1 is well established, the neuron and plasticity models in Sections 2–3 are standard, but the claims about what a column computes (Sections 4–6) are theories under active debate. The pages say which is which.

Start small and validate each layer of the model before stacking the next: a single LIF neuron that matches its analytic firing rate; an excitatory–inhibitory population that fires asynchronously and irregularly; a competitive layer that learns with STDP and homeostasis; minicolumns with dendritic segments that learn sequences; a location signal and feature-location learning; then several columns that vote. Section 7's "Step-by-Step Roadmap" turns this into a staged plan with a check at each stage, and "Common Pitfalls" lists what usually goes wrong.
